title: Emergency hub placement with a neutral-atom quantum computer
authors: Sara Tarquini, Matteo Vandelli, Francesco Ferrari, Daniele Dragoni, Francesco Tudisco
abstract: We study the problem of emergency operation center placement in disaster response, where a minimal number of hubs must be selected to ensure timely coverage of all affected locations. This task can be formulated as a minimum dominating set problem on a graph encoding reachability within a target response time. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical approximation framework that leverages neutral-atom quantum computers as independent set samplers. Candidate dominating sets are constructed from both small maximal independent sets and complements of large independent sets, and are subsequently refined via a lightweight classical procedure. We benchmark the approach on synthetic instances and realistic case studies, and implement it on the Fresnel quantum processor by Pasqal, solving instances of up to 100 nodes. Our results show that quantum-generated samples, despite hardware noise, enable near-optimal solutions of the placement problem. Overall, our results demonstrate that neutral-atom devices operating in analog mode can already be used to tackle graph optimization problems for real-world applications.
summary: The research tackles the critical emergency hub placement problem by modeling it as finding a Minimum Dominating Set on a graph. They propose and test a hybrid algorithm that uses neutral-atom quantum computers to sample candidate solutions (Independent Sets). The results show that even with hardware noise, this approach yields near-optimal solutions for large, realistic graphs, validating the use of current analog quantum devices for practical optimization tasks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the NP-hard Minimum Dominating Set (mDS) problem, framed as optimizing emergency hub placement in disaster response scenarios.
main_result: The authors demonstrated that using neutral-atom quantum computers operating in analog mode can generate near-optimal solutions for this graph optimization problem on real-world instances up to 100 nodes.
method: A hybrid quantum-classical framework is proposed, where the neutral-atom QPU samples candidate Independent Sets (IS), which are then used via classical post-processing and refinement steps to approximate the mDS.
model_or_system: The physical platform utilized is a neutral-atom quantum computer (specifically mentioning Pasqal's Fresnel processor). The computation relies on the Rydberg blockade mechanism, which naturally constrains the system's low-energy subspace to represent valid independent sets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Case studies of emergency hub placement in the Po Valley area near Modena (left) and in north-western Sicily, including Palermo (right). Graph nodes represent municipalities that are candidate locations for the placement of EOCs. Edges connect pairs of locations which lie within the given travel time Tmax. Red nodes denote the optimal solution of the mDS problem (1) on these graphs. The bottom-left insets of both panels show the embedding of each problem graph in the neutral-atom QPU chamber, corresponding to the associated atomic register.
Figure 2: Two-branch workflow for approximating the minimum dominating set (mDS) from sampled maximal independent sets (mIS), obtained either by classical or quantum methods.

Figure 3: Boxplot of the approximation ratios found by each branch of the proposed algorithm, ρmIS and ρIS [see Equation (9)], as a function of graph size |V |. We collect statistics on 30 test instances of increasing size up to |V | = 100 on randomly generated unit-disk graphs. The upper panel shows results obtained by sampling mISs classically, while the lower panel shows those obtained with the emulated quantum sampler.

Figure 4: Mean and maximum sizes of the independent sets obtained with the quantum and classical samplers. We show their average (dots) and the standard deviation (shaded area) across the instances used for the statistical experiments summarized in Figure 3. The dashed black line indicates the size of the largest mIS, averaged over the various instances.

Figure 5: Left panel: frequency of invalid (i.e., non-IS) samples f¬IS among raw bitstrings from the emulated quantum algorithm. Right panel: severity of the IS violation among non-IS samples, as measured by the number of violating edges Nviol. Statistics are collected over the same instances used for Figure 3.
